reason: E2 directly shows Pt nanoparticles remain stable on wrinkled edge planes of T-graphite up to 1173 K, supporting the anchoring premise. However, the hypothesis extends this to a general HEA/carbon system and claims a specific mechanism (high binding energy lowering mobility) and a quantitative defect-density threshold, neither of which is directly evidenced in E1 or E2. E1 only mentions thermal stability up to 1173 K without linking it to defect density. The premises about low-defect supports and degradation resistance are not supported by the cited passages.
premises: Nanoparticles are stable on edge planes of turbostratic graphite at high temperatures
High density of specific surface defects (vacancy clusters, wrinkled edge planes) provides strong anchoring
Strong anchoring minimizes nanoparticle mobility and prevents sintering
Supports with low defect density lead to sintering under thermal stress
Defect-rich supports resist moderate support degradation
